content: Mannose is a sugar monomer that belongs to the hexose series of carbohydrates. In terms of metabolism, mannose enters the carbohydrate metabolic pathway through two distinct steps: Initially, mannose undergoes phosphorylation by the enzyme hexokinase, resulting in the formation of mannose-6-phosphate. Subsequently, mannose-6-phosphate is converted into fructose-6-phosphate by the action of the enzyme mannose phosphate isomerase. Mannose can be synthesized through the oxidation of mannitol. Additionally, it can be derived from D-glucose via the Lobry-de Bruyn-van Ekenstein transformation. The term mannose shares its etymological root with mannitol, both of which originate from manna. According to biblical accounts, manna was the food provided to the Israelites during their journey through the Sinai Peninsula. Manna is a sweet secretion produced by certain trees and shrubs, such as Fraxinus ornus. D-mannose, which is naturally present in some fruits, including cranberries, has been demonstrated to inhibit the adhesion of bacteria to the tissues of the urinary tract and bladder. The configuration of D-mannose is characterized by the same stereochemical arrangement at its penultimate carbon as D-glyceraldehyde, which is consistent with its classification as a member of the dextro family of sugars. However, mannose differs from D-glucose due to the inversion of the chiral center at carbon 2 (C2). This seemingly minor structural difference results in significantly distinct chemical properties between mannose and glucose, as well as among the other six hexoses.
